description_full: Empire State Realty Trust, Inc. is a NYC-focused REIT that owns and operates a portfolio of well-leased, top of tier, modernized, amenitized, and well-located office, retail, and multifamily assets. The Company is a recognized leader in energy efficiency and indoor environmental quality. As of June 30, 2026, ESRT's portfolio is comprised of approximately 7.5 million rentable square feet of office space, 0.8 million rentable square feet of retail space and 743 residential units. Empire State Realty Trust, Inc. was established on July 29, 2011, and was incorporated in 2011 in Maryland and is based in New York.
ceo_bio: Mr. Anthony E. Malkin | Chairman & CEO | Age 63 | Compensation: $3.2M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 642 people. Revenue per employee of $1.2M ranks in the below the sector median among Real Estate peers, with revenue growing 12%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $79K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $39K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Empire State Realty Trust, Inc. is a small-cap real estate business with a $1.6B market cap on $768M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 9% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $51M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.74× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield of 2.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 8.4% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.6) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Payout ratio of 700% leaves essentially no coverage if earnings wobble
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Elevated short interest (10.1% of float) — sophisticated money is betting the other way
Interest-rate sensitivity and tenant-credit risk — cap rates and refinancing costs move faster than the 10-year leases can absorb.
Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sect: Its 18% operating margin is roughly in line with the Real Estate median (22%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.89x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 27% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 17% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.91, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.31 vs 5y 0.88), so read it loosely.
About $17.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash and 36% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 18% below its DCF fair value of $6.55, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $1.86 to $26.78 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 11.8 vs 16.3, richer on P/E 89.5 vs 24.4 and P/FCF 30.8 vs 17.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 45% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $5.50 on average, 2% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 9.1% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow, or 3% after stock compensation.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 7%.
ROE of 4% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (4.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.3% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.61 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.9% over 3 years, 4.7% over 5 years and 1.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 57%).
At current returns, reinvesting 3% of profits supports about 0.6% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -8.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 6.4% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 25.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 8.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 2.0% a year to shareholders (0.5% in buybacks and 2.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 700% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 10.1% of the float, 3.3 days to cover.
people: With about 642 employees, each generates about $1.2M of revenue, 0.5x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 11.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $79K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.2M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
